extracted.intended_audience: administrative law practitioners, UIC officials, claimants, union representatives, and researchers interested in unemployment insurance appeals (Canada)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive rules governing appeals from Boards of Referees to the Umpire under the Unemployment Insurance Act — who may appeal, when and how appeals are filed, standards of review, effects of appeals, publication and dissemination of Umpire decisions, and related practical practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Umpire jurisdiction (final level)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Umpire is the final level of appeal for litigation regarding unemployment insurance benefits (sec. 100 of the Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although final, the Umpire's quantitative intervention is limited; decisions carry weight as caselaw and are used as precedents by UIC officials and Boards of Referees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of review — law not fact (standard of review)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Umpire has jurisdiction over matters of law and not of fact, unless the interpretation of the facts by the Board of Referees seems manifestly erroneous or illogical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is the product of long jurisprudential evolution and is universally respected; the Umpire will not re-examine facts unless a serious error in interpretation is found (cf. CUB 3282).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial powers of the Umpire
rubrics_metrics.description: The appeal procedure allows the appeal tribunal to rescind or modify the decision under dispute by substituting its own decision, and the Umpire may direct the Board of Referees to reconsider or rehear the case either generally or on any particular issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal to the Umpire also has the character of an application for rehearing; scope is broad but subject-matter circumscribed by the standard of review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-requisite of Board of Referees appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal to the Umpire involves contesting a decision of the Board of Referees; it is not possible to approach the Umpire directly to contest a decision of the UIC. The appeal to the Board of Referees is a pre-requisite for appeal to the Umpire (CUB 2601).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant must first follow the Board of Referees process before seeking Umpire review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may appeal — associations' absolute right
rubrics_metrics.description: Associations of workers or associations of employers (sec. 95(b) of the Act) enjoy an absolute right to appeal decisions of the Board of Referees to the Umpire, provided the association is affected by the litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 97 lays down conditions for being 'affected' (see membership timing requirement); if entitlement to appeal is contested, the Umpire decides on the existence of the right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may appeal — claimant/employer conditional right
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimant and the employer who are directly interested have only a conditional right of appeal (sec. 95(c)), contingent on (a) the Board's decision being a majority (not unanimous) decision, or (b) the chairman of the Board granting leave to appeal against a unanimous decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automatic right of appeal inherent in a minority decision applies only to questions on which the minority member dissociated himself (CUB 3161). Because most Board decisions are unanimous, this condition significantly limits appeals by individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association affected — membership timing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For an association to be considered 'affected' (sec. 97), the claimant (or employer) must have been a member of the association both on the day employment was terminated and on the day of the appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requirement for membership on the day of appeal has been criticized as disadvantaging some unionized workers who cease membership soon after employment termination; disputes on entitlement are for the Umpire to decide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave to appeal — chairman's statutory test
rubrics_metrics.description: The chairman can grant leave only 'if it appears to him that there is a principle of importance involved in the case or if there are other special circumstances by reason of which leave to appeal ought to be granted' (sec. 96).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chairman must state reasons in writing; there is no direct right of appeal from his decision, and practice suggests many applications for leave are rejected (one chairman estimated ~60% rejected).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure and timing for leave requests
rubrics_metrics.description: When the decision is unanimous, the claimant or employer must apply to the chairman of the Board which heard the initial appeal for leave to appeal. The application for leave must be requested within 30 days unless extended by the UIC (sec. 96(1) and reg. 183(1)). The chairman must notify the UIC of his decision within 15 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submission of an application for leave is regarded as equivalent to filing an appeal, so the 45-day outer time limit (30 + 15) does not cause lapse; in practice, UIC and Umpires often accommodate delays by chairmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing deadlines for appeals to Umpire
rubrics_metrics.description: The normal time for appeal is within sixty days of the day the claimant is notified of the decision (sec. 98). This deadline can be extended only by the Umpire for special reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is dispute about the notification date, certification by the UIC that the decision was sent by mail is evidence that it was received in the ordinary course (sec. 120(2)); Umpire has discretion to extend for special reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of appeals — suspensive/stay effects
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal to the Umpire has certain staying effects; sec. 103 and reg. 167 specify conditions under which an appeal filed by the UIC can suspend implementation of a Board decision in the claimant's favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The UIC's practice is to treat appeals filed by claimants or unions against decisions requiring refund of overpayments as having a suspensive effect regarding recovery steps pending the Umpire's decision; reimbursement of expenses is only when claimant is summoned to hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility and simplicity of initiating appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The appeal to the Umpire is simpler to initiate than ordinary court appeals: it is initiated by filing a notice with the local UIC office (reg. 184(2)), not at the appeal body's headquarters; there is an absence of formality (sec. 93(1)) and it costs nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The office of the Umpire attempts to hold sessions near appellants' residences to minimize travel costs; however expenses are reimbursed only when summoned to hear, and general accessibility features reflect the administrative tribunal character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making up the file — formal filing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An appellant (individual or association) must file at the local office of the UIC which made the initial decision a written notice stating the grounds of appeal (reg. 184(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appeal procedure for members of the public falls into phases: leave to appeal (if required), making up the file, and preparations for the hearing handled by the office of the Umpire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chairman's limits and non-delegation
rubrics_metrics.description: The chairman's authority to grant or refuse leave to appeal is conferred ex officio and he cannot delegate it to a member of the Board or to another Board chairman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another chairman who has not heard the case is considered not in a position to evaluate implications or special circumstances (cf. CUB 3751).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial unanimity rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When part of the Board's decision is unanimous and part is a majority, the chairman need decide on leave only with regard to the unanimous points; majority points carry their own automatic right of appeal where applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim has been examined by several Boards, only the chairman of the last Board to hear the case may decide on leave for unanimous decisions (CUB 3686).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chairman's decision challenged at Umpire hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Although there is no right of appeal from the chairman's decision to refuse leave, the UIC may challenge at the hearing before the Umpire the granting of leave; substantial caselaw (list of CUB numbers) testifies to the effectiveness of this defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates an imbalance since the claimant must go to Federal Court to contest the chairman while UIC can raise the issue in the Umpire hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of Umpire decisions — selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Umpire decisions are recorded and may be published in full or summary if the UIC considers it appropriate (reg. 186). The Directorate selects decisions of particular interest: those concerning novel situations or which clarify doubtful or controversial interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no obligation to publish all decisions; where a series of identical decisions exists, only one may be selected for publication; editors write summaries of facts and points of law when a decision is selected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation and bilingual publication requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions and summaries are translated because the Official Languages Act requires simultaneous publication in both official languages; decisions are written in claimant's chosen official language and translated by the federal Translation Bureau.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translation capacity constraints cause considerable delays (about eighteen months) in publishing decisions; English and French versions are published separately in separate collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of access to caselaw — three sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Three ways to access Umpire caselaw: (1) the official report (CUB report) providing actual text; (2) the 'Digest of Benefit Entitlement Principles' (loose-leaf manual for UIC Agents I & II); (3) the 'Entitlement Determination Bulletin'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the CUB report gives access to most significant decisions' texts. The Digest is a practical work instrument, not a scientific research tool—lacks comprehensive indexing and hasn't been updated regularly (not amended since end of 1973). The Bulletin sometimes comments but doesn't reprint full texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digest composition and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Digest compiles law derived from the Act, Regulations and caselaw across ~20 major topics; text often juxtaposes verbatim quotations, references, and transitional passages that make statements of principle without indicating sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digest intended as a manual for decision-makers (Agents) to decide issues with minimal research; it is not intended as an exhaustive or fully-sourced research resource. Lack of index and dated updates limit its use as authoritative precedent-finder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Umpires' adherence to precedent and panels
rubrics_metrics.description: Umpire decisions are rigorously adhered to by UIC officials and Boards of Referees; individual Umpires do not feel equally bound by their own prior decisions unless the question has consistent jurisprudence or a decision by a panel of Umpires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A panel decision (e.g., CUB 3399) is regarded as a definitive pronouncement; absent consistent prior rulings or panel decision, Umpires sometimes adopt divergent positions though they strive for mutual compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal dissemination practice of Umpire decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a decision is recorded and filed, a copy is sent to the Directorate of Insurance; after checking fidelity and collecting ~10 bilingual decisions they print and distribute internally (Regional Offices, District Offices, Boards, law schools, unions, claimant assistance agencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Official public publication occurs later after collecting ~100 decisions via government printing office; volumes have 200–300 decisions, no index, cited by number with no date indication, limiting usability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical selection and effect of leave requirement on appeal flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Because most Board decisions are unanimous (practically ~95%), the need to obtain leave to appeal markedly reduces the flow of individual appeals to the Umpire; data from late 1974 show roughly half of appeals by individuals involved unanimous Board decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, the leave requirement results in selection bias of cases reaching the Umpire and influences caseload composition; unions taking up cases can bypass leave requirements.
